---
title: Model candidates
---

#### 🧭 Purpose

*Compare documented model configurations with the current outcome, predictor types,
missing values and observation structure. Use this diagnostic card after data
preparation, before choosing a model to train. The upstream Observation resampling
plan, when present, determines which internal-resampling recipes are included.*

The card displays recipes from the versioned capability catalogue. It does not fit,
benchmark, install or automatically select a model, and it leaves incoming data and
pipeline metadata unchanged until Commit is pressed.

#### 🎯 Goals

1. **Primary:** Find recipes that meet the current data requirements.
2. **Secondary:** Explain exclusions, unknown capabilities and preparation requirements.
3. **Tertiary:** Distinguish runtime evidence from documentation and expert judgment.

#### 🧠 How it works

The outcome task comes from the upstream modeling context. Automatic inference uses
a numeric Target for regression, a nominal or Boolean Target for classification, and
an ordered categorical Target for ordinal classification. Numeric class codes need
an explicit classification choice upstream. Without a resolved outcome, the card
asks for a Target or an explicit task.

Only Predictor-role columns are inspected. Target and declared survival outcome
components are excluded. Treatment, Identifier, Sequence, Geometry and Weighting
columns are not silently added to the design matrix. Assign predictor roles
intentionally when defining the analysis.

The card distinguishes missing numeric and missing categorical values. Boolean and
ordered categorical predictors request categorical support; preserving ordinal order
is a recipe-specific consideration. Infinite numeric values and unsupported types,
such as raw datetime predictors, prevent a compatible match until prepared upstream.

The **Implicit resampling** column describes internal validation/tuning splits in
the recorded recipe. Bootstrap training and subsampling do not count. With an
upstream evaluation plan defined, recipes using internal splits are excluded.
Without an upstream plan, recipes without internal splits are excluded. Enable
**Show excluded and unreviewed recipes** to see both groups and their reasons;
excluded recipes cannot be committed or restored as committed models.

This is reviewed recipe information, not a name-suffix test. For example,
`ElasticNetCV` performs internal tuning and `NuSVC(probability=True)` performs
internal probability calibration. Automatic early stopping can depend on training
size; conditional and unreviewed configurations remain excluded until their split
behavior is established. A small histogram-boosting recipe with no internal split
is marked No; with more than 10,000 rows and no upstream plan it is marked Yes.
With an upstream plan on larger data its status is Conditional because fitting
sizes may differ across folds and transformations. Upstream samplers that may
expand the training data also make automatic early stopping Conditional. Internal validation does not
by itself supply an independent assessment of the final selected model, nor does
it guarantee suitable time/group restrictions. Other readiness and evidence rules
continue to apply, so the included table may be empty.

Each row describes one joint configuration. A model that handles categories only
after encoding is shown with its input requirements; capabilities from separate recipes
are never combined. Readiness combines input and broader requirements: Meets requirements, specific
preprocessing actions, unsupported requirements, or Untested. With excluded models
hidden, every displayed row meets requirements. Evidence remains separate. Requirements describe the
needed result, such as numeric representations or no missing values, without
prescribing imputation or one-hot encoding. The flip-side separately records the
specific tested preparation. Alternative techniques may satisfy the requirements,
but are not validated by that recorded probe. Compatibility and evidence continue
to refer to the complete tested recipe, not the bare estimator. Identifier repetition, Sequence and Geometry roles introduce
longitudinal, temporal and spatial requirements. Content that merely looks like a
date or coordinate does not establish those roles.

| Status | Interpretation |
|:--|:--|
| Meets requirements | Current inputs and broader requirements meet the checks performed here. |
| Preprocessing: … | Resolve the stated input conditions before fitting. |
| Does not support … | A required capability is explicitly unsupported. |
| Untested: … | At least one input condition, capability or structural use has not been reviewed. |
| Probe passed | The recorded configuration passed small compatibility checks. |
| Documentation only | Official documentation was reviewed; adapters and runtime probes remain outstanding. |

Installation/version status is independent of these judgments. A missing optional
package does not mean its model is analytically unsuitable. A matching package
version does not validate an untested adapter.

#### 🏞️ Front

The summary names the task, structural requirements and predictor count. The table
shows model, input requirements, readiness, evidence, installation and scale guidance. Column filters help narrow the displayed rows. Fullscreen gives
the table more vertical space.

The table columns are ordered: Model, Core mechanism, Composition, Fitting criterion, Transparency, Learning strategy, Prediction outputs, Pred throughput, Scale, Input requirements, Implicit resampling, Readiness, Evidence, Package, Installation, and Recipes.

Each table row represents one method. Recipes counts the recipes remaining after the display filters. A single ranked recipe supplies the row’s readiness, evidence, requirements and installation status. Matching, validated recipes are preferred for the summary. Capabilities are never combined across recipes. On the flip side, expand each recipe to compare its own preparation, conditions and evidence. Enable Show excluded and unreviewed recipes to inspect alternatives hidden by the current requirements.

Select a row, then flip the card to inspect it. An empty table is explained in the
footer. It may mean insufficient catalogue coverage rather than absence of suitable
models in the wider ecosystem.

#### 🔄 Flip side

The flip side presents the selected recipe in a shaded panel with a readable model
name, a separate technical identifier, and distinct readiness and evidence badges.
Input requirements, tested preparation, configuration, fitting instructions,
conditions, assessment and references are grouped into sections. The panel scrolls
in the compact card and uses additional columns when space permits in full-screen.
Judgments are guidance, not measured accuracy or timing results.

Readiness combines current input and broader requirements; evidence describes the
complete tested recipe. This card never trains models or executes preparation.
Catalogue coverage is incomplete, and documentation-only recipes need adapters and
runtime validation. A valid upstream resampling plan is needed before evaluation,
but the catalogue remains browsable without one. Data-specific warnings, including
weighting fallbacks, appear beside the front summary rather than in a separate
flip-side Notes block.

#### 🛠️ Controls and actions

- **Show excluded and unreviewed recipes:** Include superseded, incompatible and unknown recipes
  for the current task, with reasons. Superseded entries name the broader method;
  the flip side explains parameter mappings and limitations. This is display grouping,
  not automatic model substitution. This does not list every unreviewed estimator
  in the raw inventory; entries need a recipe.
- **Show installed packages only:** Hide packages absent from the current environment.
  Installed versions may still differ from the reviewed snapshot.
- **Use observation weightings:** Require fitting-weight support when the assigned
  effective weights are valid and nonuniform. Invalid weights produce a visible
  unweighted fallback; this card does not apply weights or rebalance data.
- **Explore forecasting recipes:** Browse forecasting contracts explicitly. Sequence
  supplies time-index metadata, but forecast horizons and lag windows still require
  a future adapter. A resampling window is not automatically a forecasting horizon.
- **Required prediction output:** Request probabilities, survival risk, a forecast or
  prediction intervals. Unreviewed output support is shown as unknown.

Settings affect display and matching only and use ordinary card configuration
persistence. There is no training or apply button.

#### 🔎 Interpretation and next steps

Review preparation and assumptions before choosing a candidate. A survival risk
ranking and a survival probability curve are different outputs. Spatial fitted
values do not establish prediction support at new locations. A repeated-entity model
may require different prediction rules for known and unseen subjects.

#### ⛔️ Limitations

The catalogue is intentionally incomplete. Specialist recipes currently require
integration work and runtime validation. Predictor summaries describe the current
preview; preprocessing must be refitted within each training fold. A compatible row
does not certify task assumptions, valid metrics, calibration, runtime, memory use or
out-of-sample accuracy. The card does not infer a spatial weights matrix, forecast
horizon or lag configuration. Evaluation readiness remains separate from browsing.

#### 📌 Suggested workflow

1. Assign roles and confirm outcome semantics upstream.
2. Define and inspect an evaluation plan in Observation resampling.
3. Review compatible recipes and their preparation.
4. Show excluded/unreviewed recipes to understand coverage gaps.
5. Inspect the selected recipe and validate it in the eventual training workflow.

#### 🔗 Data flow

- **Input:** Current predictors, stable outcome data, roles, modeling context and
  evaluation metadata, plus the JSON catalogue and installed-package metadata.
- **Output:** Until commitment, the incoming proxy passes through unchanged. Commit adds an unfitted terminal estimator recipe to the pipeline and a Learning entry to the data journey; data values remain unchanged.
- **Data journey:** No cleaning operation, learned transformation or evaluation plan
  is added. Display changes do not train models or start extended tasks.

#### 🧭 Model characteristics

Six descriptive columns help compare methods: **Core mechanism**, **Composition**,
**Fitting criterion**, **Learning strategy**, **Prediction outputs**, and **Transparency**.
Use the column headings to sort the table. Scroll horizontally to reach
additional columns; select a row and flip the card for explanations and sources.
Sorting changes the view, not the data or model configuration.

- **Core mechanism** permits combinations, such as Tree and Gen. linear.
  **Gen. linear** means linear / generalized linear, including linear predictors
  over transformed features. Distribution, rule, symbolic, prototype and specialist
  mechanisms are retained where the initial families do not describe a method.
- **Composition** describes how components combine: a forest aggregates trees;
  a model tree routes to linear leaf models. Multiple labels can describe nested
  composition. A component's transparency does not automatically transfer to its
  ensemble.
- **Fitting criterion** distinguishes loss, regularization and split criteria in
  the details. It can be configuration dependent; some neighborhood methods do
  not optimize a fitting loss. Model-selection criteria are not fitting losses.
- **Learning strategy** describes when the predictor is constructed. **Eager**
  methods fit a reusable model before prediction; **Lazy** methods defer local
  estimation or neighbor aggregation until each query; **Hybrid** methods combine
  both predictive mechanisms. Nearest-neighbor predictors are Lazy even when they
  build a search index or use ordinary preprocessing. Nearest-centroid, GP and SVM
  predictors are Eager: retaining training data or doing substantial prediction-time
  computation does not make a method lazy. Configurable wrappers say **Depends on
  configuration** until a recipe resolves their components. This is not a speed
  ranking, memory guarantee or incremental-learning flag. Sort this column and
  inspect the recipe details for its qualification.
- **Prediction outputs** combines the former Formulation and Prediction outputs
  descriptions. Regression recipes show **Point prediction** or **Point prediction
  & spread**. Spread means a documented uncertainty output for individual predictions,
  such as predictive standard deviation, covariance, intervals or distribution samples;
  it does not certify calibration. Gaussian-process regression, Bayesian ridge and ARD
  regression provide point predictions and spread. Their details identify the output
  options and the meaning of that uncertainty.
  Ordinary linear-regression recipes remain **Point prediction** because these recipes
  return point predictions only. This is a recipe capability distinction: some other
  OLS implementations can calculate input-dependent prediction intervals.
  A single fitted quantile, coefficient standard errors, global residual variance or
  variation among ensemble members alone do not establish prediction-spread support.
  The flip side retains the precise output list, including quantiles and specialist
  outputs. Classification still distinguishes labels, scores and class probabilities.
  Use **Required prediction output: Prediction spread** to require spread support.
- **Transparency** is expert guidance about the whole model: Usually transparent,
  Conditional, or Usually opaque. Complexity, transformed features and composition
  can change how understandable a fitted model is. It is not a measured score or
  a claim about post-hoc explanation tools.

**Unreviewed**, **Not applicable**, and **Depends on configuration** have distinct
meanings. A method summary says **Varies by recipe** when its displayed recipes
have different descriptions; inspect each recipe rather than pooling their
capabilities. Readiness and evidence still describe the named summary recipe.
The characteristics do not establish compatibility, installation, integration,
or successful validation. **Capacity growth** is reserved for stage 2 and is not
currently assessed or displayed as a filter.

### Committing a model

Select a method and press **Commit**. The displayed summary recipe is committed, including its constructor parameters and supported preparation. The status beneath the button identifies the committed estimator and recipe. You can select a different row at any time; the status identifies this pending choice and asks you to Commit to replace the model. Browsing alone does not replace a committed model. Changing upstream data requires a fresh commitment.

JSON configuration saves the selected method and recipe separately from the committed recipe. Loading it restores the selected row by stable method identity, independent of its numeric row position or sort order, and rebuilds the committed model without fitting it. Restoration rechecks compatibility and construction support; an unavailable or incompatible saved recipe is reported rather than replaced with another model. A restored row remains freely changeable. Older configurations that did not record a model choice still require a selection and commitment.

Commit does not fit a model. The pipeline selects predictor-role columns before the estimator, excluding outcomes and other non-predictor roles. Supported preparation is fitted only when the pipeline is trained. Unvalidated, unavailable, or adapter-dependent recipes cannot be committed; the footer explains the reason and retains any previous commitment. Weighting requirements remain catalogue checks; training consumers must supply fit weights explicitly.


#### Learning strategy and prediction speed

**Eager** means that fitting constructs reusable predictive quantities before
queries arrive. **Lazy** means that local estimation or neighbor aggregation is
deferred until a prediction query. **Hybrid** combines both predictive mechanisms.
These labels describe when learning happens, not how much time each stage takes.

Gaussian processes are Eager: training computes reusable posterior quantities,
but prediction still involves the training observations. They can therefore be
expensive both to fit and to predict. Building a neighbor-search index does not
make a nearest-neighbor predictor Eager; its predictive aggregation still happens
at query time.

Documentation can support a broad **expected prediction throughput** assessment
(Low, Medium or High), provided it is explicitly labelled documentation-based,
conditional on model size and workload, and accompanied by its reason. High
would mean more predictions per second, not higher computational cost. A reliable
numerical rate or a defensible comparison for the chosen pipeline requires a
performance benchmark. The **Pred throughput** column shows these qualitative model-only ratings for the
representative recipe: **High** for compact prediction calculations, **Medium**
for moderate or configuration-dependent inference work, and **Low** for methods
whose query work commonly grows with retained training observations or support
vectors. These are documentation-informed judgments, not categories assigned by
the documentation or measured rates. Reasons, assumptions and source links are
stored in `prediction_throughput.json`; they are omitted from the table. New or
changed, unreviewed recipes show Unreviewed rather than a guessed rating. Ratings
do not affect eligibility, search ranking or model acceptance.

For example, a small linear predictor generally involves less prediction work
than an ensemble with many deep trees. Exact Gaussian-process and kernel-model
prediction costs depend on the retained training observations or support vectors.
These observations describe scaling, not universal speed rankings. Hardware,
thread settings, feature count, sparsity, requested output (such as probabilities
or predictive uncertainty), preprocessing and batch size can change the result.
See [scikit-learn's computational-performance guidance](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/computing/computational_performance.html).

A future downstream performance card could benchmark the fitted model and the
complete inference pipeline separately, reporting both single-observation latency
and batch throughput. Repeat warmed-up measurements and record batch size,
requested output, model size, hardware and thread configuration. Generate any
stochastic benchmark inputs before timing; preserve feature types, valid category
levels, plausible ranges, missingness and relevant dependencies. Include
representative held-out input rows where available: independent random values
alone may exercise unrealistic prediction paths. This would measure inference
performance, not predictive accuracy, and must not refit the model or execute
training-only resampling while timing predictions.


CatBoost recipes can be committed for entirely numeric data as well as mixed
inputs. The recipe name `catboost_strings` describes its optional categorical
preparation; it does not require string predictors. Numeric columns remain
numeric, including numeric missing values. When categorical predictors are present,
the pipeline deterministically converts their values to typed strings and uses a
separate missing token that cannot collide with a real value. The CatBoost adapter
identifies categorical columns from the actual training-fold design, including
any upstream feature selection. Browsing or committing still performs no fit.


#### Multiple candidate methods

Select one or more method rows (Ctrl/Command-click adds rows) and press **Commit**.
All selected methods are validated before the candidate set is committed; an
invalid recipe leaves the previous commitment intact. One applicable recipe is
retained per selected method. Details describe the first selected method.

Proxy-data stores stable recipe IDs, method names and independent unfitted model
pipelines, including each method's preparation. These are alternative endings,
not an ensemble. Shared upstream transformations stay outside the alternatives.
With one candidate, ordinary training behaves as before. With several candidates,
a consumer must choose a candidate explicitly or use Pipeline tuning; the first
candidate is never silently used for training. Configuration JSON preserves both
the selected method list and the committed recipe list. Legacy single-method
configuration fields remain readable. Changing upstream data requires recommitment.

Accepted outputs expose the final method ID through `selected_model_candidate`; the stored alternatives remain available through `model_candidates`.
